question.text: This "Commodore" made his initial money in the shipping industry, but later made his fortune in the railroad industry. He is also the namesake of a Tennessee university.
question.clue: This man served as a business manager for Thomas Gibbons before clashing with Daniel Drew over use of the Hudson River.

swap.text: Achieving bimetallism was one of the goals of this party, whose policies would benefit farmers and the common folk.
swap.clue: A vice-presidential candidate for this party was a champion of Rural Free Delivery named Thomas E. Watson.

question.text: The Tenure of Office Act also prevented President Hayes from firing this man, who earned his job from Roscoe Conkling via the patronage system. As President, this successor of James Garfield would pass the Pendleton Act to end patronage.
question.clue: This president vetoed a bill sponsored by California's John F. Miller on grounds that it violated the Burlingame Treaty, but ultimately signed a compromise Chinese Exclusion Act into law.

swap.text: During his second term, Cleveland sent in troops to put down this 1894 strike based on his constitutional responsibility to have mail delivered. This railroad strike was led by Eugene V. Debs.
swap.clue: Governor John Atgeld was opposed to the federal response to this event, which occurred after the disruption of the mail service.

question.leadin: This speech claims that "the attorney in a country town is as much a businessman as the corporation counsel in a great metropolis."
question.text: Name this speech delivered at the 1896 Democratic National Convention that warns business interests not to "press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns."
question.clue: This speech urged the masses not to "press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns" in a condemnation of the gold standard.

swap.leadin: In this battle, Admiral Patricio Montojo ["mont-o-ho"] was forced to abandon the Reina Cristina and hoist his flag on the cruiser Isla de Cuba.
swap.text: Name this decisive naval battle, also known as the Battle of Cavite ["cah-vee-tay"].
swap.clue: The fighting took place around Sangley Point and commenced with the enemy's abandonment of its flagship, the Queen Christina.

question.leadin: This structure was funded by the Western Pacific, Central Pacific, and Union Pacific Railway Companies.
question.text: Name this 1869 railroad that succeeded in connecting much of the Eastern and Western United States.
question.clue: This entity was financed by the Big Four, which included Leland Stanford.

swap.leadin: This man had a spat with Rutherford B. Hayes over patronage at a Customs House.
swap.text: Name this leader of the Stalwarts, who opposed the Half-Breed's calls for Civil Service reform. He was the mentor of Chester Arthur.
swap.clue: He had resigned over the appointment of William Robertson as Collector of the Port of New York by James Garfield, which was presumably a violation of the Treaty of Fifth Avenue that the faction he led agreed to with the Half-Breeds.

question.leadin: Name these business regulation cases from the nineteenth century Supreme Court.
question.text: This 1876 ruling arising out of Illinois found that states had the power to set maximum rates for grain storage.
question.clue: That opinion also uses the examples of wharfingers and hackney-coachmen and quotes Lord Hale's De Portibus Maris to show that the legislation in question did not violate the due process clause.

swap.leadin: Name these Republican factions from the late nineteenth century.
swap.text: This Algonquin word referred to Republicans who refused to support party nominee James Blaine against Grover Cleveland in 1884.
swap.clue: Dorman Eaton was another member of this group, which had been alienated by the scandal involving the Little Rock and Fort Smith Railroads, and was denounced in a tirade by the Reverend Samuel Burchard.

question.text: Macdonald resigned at prime minister in 1873 due to the Pacific Scandal, a series of allegations of bribery stemming from Canada's construction of one of these.
question.clue: North American types of these projects depended on cheap coolies from China and frequently had the word "Pacific" in their names.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about coinage in US history.
swap.text: This act, passed in 1890, increased the amount of silver that the US government was required to buy by four and a half million ounces with notes that could be redeemed with either silver or gold-- a fact exploited by investors leading to the Panic of 1893.
swap.clue: Democrats who supported the repeal of this act formed a presidential ticket of Simon Bolivar Buckner and John Palmer that received 1% of the vote.

question.text: This leader of operations for Carnegie Steel locked the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel works out of the plant.
question.clue: Joseph Duveen advised this man on purchasing works like Vermeer's Officer and Laughing Girl for his Fifth Avenue mansion.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the life and times of Schuyler Colfax.
swap.text: Although his term as Vice President was up anyways, Colfax saw his political career end as a result of this scandal, which involved the bribery of officials by a fake company set up by Union Pacific.
swap.clue: Peter A. Day was fired for providing ungenerous estimates in this scandal, while James Brooks was censured in the investigation following its exposure.

question.text: This influential newspaper editor attempted to intervene on behalf of the strikers. He took over the New York Tribune from Horace Greeley, and replaced Levi Morton as Benjamin Harrison's VP nominee in the 1892 election.

swap.leadin: In a case concerning these businesses, a New Orleans Benevolent Association sued the monopolistic company Crescent City, a corporation established by the Louisiana legislature.
swap.text: Name these businesses that named a series of cases ruling that the Privileges and Immunities Clause protected only federal citizens.
swap.answerHtml: slaughterhouses [accept meatpacking factories or meat processing factories; prompt on factories]
swap.clue: In a case named for these places, Associate Justice Samuel Miller ruled that the Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment applied only to federal citizenship and not the states.

question.leadin: This man's early distinctions included being chosen president of the International Sanitary Conference, and he got his start as assistant to William Evarts.
question.text: Identify this author of the supposedly-not-too-bad book The Bread Winners who also played a key role in the negotiations that kept the Philippines an American possession following the Spanish-American War.
question.clue: With John George Nicolay, this man co-wrote a ten-volume biography of Abraham Lincoln based on his experience as the President's personal secretary.

swap.text: The Poland Act led to this 1878 test case, with a majority written by Chief Justice Morrison Waite. The Church allowed a man to be charged with bigamy; the Court upheld laws against polygamy against the argument that they infringed upon religious duty.
swap.clue: In this 1878 case, the Supreme Court ruled that bigamy as a Mormon religious duty was not protected under the First Amendment.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about an extremely unattractive woman, FTPE.
question.text: This author of Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist clearly had low standards, because he was Goldman's romantic partner. He wrote said memoirs while in jail for attempting to kill Henry Clay Frick after the Homestead Strike.
question.clue: This anarchist and lifelong lover of Emma Goldman, who was jailed for trying to kill Henry Frick.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about free love and the appropriately named Fanny Wright, FTPE.
swap.text: One of the biggest blows to the free love movement was the 1873 passage of this act, which banned the distribution of sexually-oriented publications in the U.S. and declared contraceptives themselves.
swap.clue: Griswold overruled Connecticut's "Little" version of this 1873 Federal law, which made it illegal to distribute "obscene" information, including information on birth control, through the mail.
